cards.front: Recall a key point about Rights & Responsibilities of Citizens
cards.back: Rights and responsibilities are two sides of the same citizenship coin. Rights: what you are entitled to (vote, free speech, fair trial, education, healthcare). Responsibilities: what you owe to society (obey the law, pay taxes, vote, serve on a jury, respect others' rights).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Rights & Responsibilities of Citizens
cards.back: Legal responsibilities: obey the law (criminal and civil law apply to all), pay taxes (income tax, VAT, council tax fund public services), and serve on a jury if called (criminal trials require 12 jurors to determine guilt). Jury service is a civic duty - you can be fined for not attending without good reason.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Rights & Responsibilities of Citizens
cards.back: Civic responsibilities: vote in elections (not legally required but considered a civic duty), engage with political issues, volunteer in the community, and treat others with respect regardless of background. These are not legally enforced but are expected of good citizens.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Rights & Responsibilities of Citizens
cards.back: The balance between rights and responsibilities: your right to free speech comes with the responsibility not to incite hatred; your right to protest comes with the responsibility to do so peacefully; your right to education comes with the responsibility to attend school until 18. Rights without responsibilities lead to selfish individualism; responsibilities without rights lead to oppression.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Rights & Responsibilities of Citizens
cards.back: Active citizenship: taking practical action to address community issues. Examples: campaigning (writing to MPs, organising petitions), volunteering (food banks, charity shops, mentoring), community action (clean-ups, neighbourhood watch), and participation (attending council meetings, joining political parties). Active citizenship is assessed as part of GCSE Citizenship Studies.

cards.front: What should you know about citizenship studies exam tips — rights & responsibilities of citizens?
cards.back: 1. For Rights & Responsibilities of Citizens questions, use citizenship terminology and reference democratic processes accurately 2. Consider multiple viewpoints — including those you disagree with 3. Link Rights & Responsibilities of Citizens to current affairs and real-world examples where possible 4. When evaluating, consider both rights and responsibilities 5. Structure longer answers: identify the issue, analyse different perspectives, reach a justified view
Evaluate the view that citizens have a duty to participate actively in their community and democracy.

cards.front: Understanding Rights & Responsibilities of Citizens in British Context
cards.back: Rights & Responsibilities of Citizens is a core topic in GCSE Citizenship Studies that requires understanding of how the UK political and legal systems work, and how citizens can participate effectively. The specification requires you to know how British democracy functions, understand your rights and responsibilities as a citizen, and be able to take informed and responsible action on citizenship

cards.front: Rights & Responsibilities of Citizens and UK Democratic Processes
cards.back: The UK is a parliamentary democracy where citizens exercise power through elected representatives. Understanding rights & responsibilities of citizens requires knowledge of how democratic processes work: general elections (first past the post), devolved elections (additional member system for Scotland and Wales), local elections, and referendums. cards.front: Rights, Responsibilities and Rights & Responsibilities of Citizens
cards.back: UK citizens have both rights and responsibilities. Key rights include: the right to vote, freedom of speech, freedom of religion, the right to a fair trial, and the right to privacy. These rights are protected by the Human Rights Act 1998, which incorporates the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law.
